subject: Career
title: French and Raven's Five Bases of Power
description: A quick, practical guide to French and Raven's Five Bases of Power.

hook.text: Your manager has power because of her title. Your colleague has power because everyone trusts her. Different sources.

buildup.text: French and Raven identified five power bases: legitimate, reward, coercive, expert, and referent.

discovery.text: Legitimate = title. Reward = can give. Coercive = can punish. Expert = knows most. Referent = is admired.

twist.text: Expert and referent power are the most durable. Positional power vanishes when you change roles.

climax.text: Build expert and referent power regardless of your title. They follow you between jobs.

punchline.text: Titles give temporary power. Expertise and trust give permanent power.

quiz.question: Which power bases are most durable according to French and Raven?

details.summary: French and Raven identified five sources of power: legitimate, reward, coercive, expert, and referent. Understanding which bases you hold and which others use helps you navigate workplace influence dynamics strategically.
details.whyItMatters: Most professionals rely on only one or two power bases without realizing it. Diversifying your power sources makes your influence more resilient and adaptable.
takeaways: Expert power comes from knowledge and is the most meritocratic base
Referent power comes from being liked and respected by others
Coercive power is the least sustainable and most relationship-damaging

faq.question: Which base of power is most effective for long-term career success?
faq.answer: Expert and referent power are the most durable because they are earned rather than assigned. Legitimate power depends on your title and can disappear with a reorganization. Expert and referent power travel with you across roles and organizations.

faq.question: Can someone with no formal authority still be powerful in a workplace?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Expert power from deep knowledge and referent power from strong relationships can make someone without a title among the most influential people in an organization. Informal power often matters more than formal authority in daily decisions.
